understand.concept: A set is an unordered collection of distinct hashable elements. Duplicate values collapse into one member. Sets support membership tests and mathematical set operations, but do not support positional indexing or slicing.
understand.whyItMatters: Python Sets is useful when a program needs to organize, inspect or transform related data reliably.
understand.analogy: A set is like a collection of unique membership cards: each item is present once, with no positional promise.
understand.analogyLimit: A set does not preserve a meaningful position for each member, and elements must be hashable.

explain.narrative:
## Python Sets

A set is an unordered collection of distinct hashable elements. Duplicate values collapse into one member. Sets support membership tests and mathematical set operations, but do not support positional indexing or slicing.

## Choosing an operation

Read the example code and check whether the operation mutates the object, returns a new value, or may raise an exception. Use membership tests and defaults where input may be missing.

## Practical reasoning

The five examples progress from basic use to a small real-world pattern. Compare each expected output with the code before changing it.

examples.expectedOutput: Duplicate red is stored once; membership tests whether a value exists.

examples.title:
empty = set()
print(type(empty).__name__)
print(len(empty))
examples.expectedOutput: Use set() for an empty set because {} creates an empty dictionary.

examples.title:
letters = set('level')
print(sorted(letters))
examples.expectedOutput: Constructing a set from a string keeps each distinct character.

examples.title:
values = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]
unique = set(values)
print(sorted(unique))
examples.expectedOutput: A set removes duplicate values; sorting is used here for predictable display.
